**Solution 1 (326) is the most likely correct answer, though I did not fully verify its sufficiency claim.**

**Necessity of 3 ∤ n.** Each operation turns exactly 3 white cells black, so the black count after k operations is 1 + 3k. Filling the board needs n² = 1 + 3k, so n² ≡ 1 (mod 3), which means 3 ∤ n. This rules out n = 3, 6, 9, …

**n = 5 is impossible.** Label cells (row, column).
- The corner (1,5) can only be coloured by the square rows 1–2, cols 4–5. At that moment exactly one of (1,4), (2,4), (2,5) must be black. Working back, the unique black cell must be (2,4), and it can only have been coloured by the square rows 2–3, cols 3–4 (every other square containing (2,4) also touches (1,4), (1,5) or (2,5)). Call this square A.
- By symmetry, the corner (5,5) forces the square rows 3–4, cols 3–4, call it B, to be applied.
- A and B overlap in (3,3) and (3,4). Applying either one turns its whole 2×2 square black, so the other then has at least two black cells forever and can never be applied.
- Both corners must be coloured, so n = 5 is impossible.

**Consequences for the candidates.**
- Solution 2 assumes every n with 3 ∤ n works, so it includes 5 and is wrong. Its sum of 300 is therefore incorrect.
- Solution 3 claims only powers of 2 work. It says n = 5 fails, which is correct, but it asserts n = 7 fails. The corner obstructions for n = 7 sit far apart and do not conflict in the same way, so 7 is plausibly possible, and Solution 3's characterization is likely wrong.
- Solution 1 excludes exactly 3 ∤ n failures plus n = 5, which matches the necessity argument above. Its list of the first 20 valid values is 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 17, 19, 20, 22, 23, 25, 26, 28, 29, 31. Adding them gives 326, which I re-checked.

I did not construct explicit colourings for n = 7 or larger, so Solution 1's sufficiency claim rests on the pattern matching the n = 5 obstruction and on n = 2 and n = 4 both working. That leaves moderate confidence.

CHOICE: 1
